'''Michael Aizenman''' ({{Langx|he|מיכאל אייזנמן}}; born 28 August 1945) is an American-Israeli [[mathematician]] and a [[physicist]] at [[Princeton University]], working in the fields of [[mathematical physics]], [[statistical mechanics]], [[functional analysis]] and [[probability theory]].

The highlights of his work include: the [[quantum triviality|triviality]] of a class of [[scalar (physics)|scalar]] [[quantum field theory|quantum field theories]] in [[extra dimensions|more than three dimensions]]; a description of the [[phase transition]] in the [[Ising model]] in three and more dimensions; the sharpness of the [[phase transition]] in [[percolation theory]]; a method for the study of spectral and dynamical localization for random [[Schrödinger operator]]s; and insights concerning [[Riemann surface|conformal invariance]] in two-dimensional percolation.<ref name="google scholar">{{cite web | title = Michael Aizenman's publications on Google Scholar | url = https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&lr=&q=Michael+Aizenman}}</ref>

==Biography==
Aizenman is a [[Jewish]]<ref name=jinfo>{{cite web |url=http://www.jinfo.org/Heineman_Physics.html |title=Jewish Recipients Of The Dannie Heineman Prize For Mathematical Physics |website=Jinfo.org |accessdate=21 July 2019}}</ref> American - Israeli who was born in Russia. He was an undergraduate at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]]. He was awarded his PhD in 1975 at [[Yeshiva University]] (Belfer Graduate School of Science), [[New York City]], with advisor [[Joel Lebowitz]]. After [[postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral]] appointments at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] of [[New York University]] (1974&ndash;75), and Princeton University (1975&ndash;1977), with [[Elliott H. Lieb]], he was appointed [[assistant professor]] at Princeton. In 1982 he moved to [[Rutgers University]] as [[associate professor]] and then [[full professor]].  In 1987 he moved to the [[Courant Institute]] and in 1990 returned to [[Princeton University|Princeton]] as professor of mathematics and physics. He was several times a [[visiting scholar]] at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], in 1984–85, 1991–92, and 1997–98,<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/ Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars]</ref> and is a regular visiting scholar at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]].

==Honors and awards==
* Norbert Wiener Prize (1990) of the [[American Mathematical Society|Amer. Math. Soc.]] and [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] for "his outstanding contribution of original and non-[[perturbative]] mathematical methods in [[statistical mechanics]] by means of which he was able to solve several long open important problems concerning critical phenomena, phase transitions, and [[quantum field theory]]."
* [[Brouwer Medal]] (2002)<ref name="Brouwer Medal laudatio">{{cite web | title = Brouwer Medal laudatio | url = http://www.math.leidenuniv.nl/~naw/serie5/deel04/jun2003/pdf/laudatio-aizenman.pdf}}</ref> of the Dutch Math. Soc. and the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences|Royal Dutch Academy of Arts and Sciences]] 
* Dannie Heineman Prize in Mathematical Physics (2010), of [[American Physics Society|APS]] and [[American Institute of Physics|AIP]]
* [[Henri Poincare Prize|Henri Poincaré Prize]] (2018) of IAMP.

Aizenman received [[honorary degree]]s (DHC) from [[Cergy-Pontoise University|Université de Cergy-Pontoise]] (2009) and [[Technion]] (2018), and is a member of
[[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (1997), [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2017), and Academia Europaea (2016).

During 2001-2012 he served as the [[editor-in-chief]] of [[Communications in Mathematical Physics]].

==Publications==
*[https://www.ams.org/bookstore-getitem/item=gsm-168 ''Random Operators: Disorder Effects on Quantum Spectra and Dynamics''], by M. Aizenman and [[Simone Warzel|S. Warzel]] (AMS 2015).
* Aizenman, Michael; [[Hugo Duminil-Copin | Duminil-Copin, Hugo]] (2021), Marginal triviality of the scaling limits of critical 4D Ising and ϕ44 models. ''Ann. of Math.'' (2) 194 (2021), no. 1, 163–235.
